title: Release audit: `bounded_run` does not make the watchdog's timeout decision authoritative. After
summary: Have the watchdog record the final child/timeout status and wait for that status before deciding success, or measure the deadline in the parent and fail on any overrun; add a test whose checked shell returns just after FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT.
requirements: `bounded_run` must not treat the absence of the `timed-out` marker at the moment the checked child exits as proof that the bound did not elapse; the timeout decision must be resolved after the watchdog has reached its own decision.
When the bound elapsed before the checked command exited, `bounded_run` must set `CHECK_STATUS=124` regardless of the ordering between the child's exit and the marker write.
`verify_profile` must report `CHECK_STATUS=124` as a failed verification: a non-zero installer exit and a message that names the configured limit, never a success.
When the checked command exits before the bound elapses, `bounded_run` must return that command's own exit status and its captured output unchanged.
Every exit path of `bounded_run` must leave no watchdog process and no private check directory behind, including the timeout path and paths taken after a failure.
The wait for the watchdog's decision must itself be bounded by a fixed, small limit derived from `VERIFY_GRACE`, so `install.sh` cannot hang waiting for a watchdog that never answers.
The installer must remain POSIX `sh` (`sh -n install.sh` clean, `set -eu`) and must not invoke GNU `timeout` or any binary not already used by the script.

A regression test in `tests/test_install.py` must exercise the real `install.sh` with a fresh-shell check whose runtime exceeds `FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT` and assert that the install fails at the bound instead of reporting success.
No existing test may be weakened to accommodate the change.
The whole existing test suite must still pass.
acceptance: A checked command that outlives `FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT` makes `install.sh` exit non-zero with a failure message naming the limit, and this holds even when the command's exit lands between the limit and the watchdog's marker write.
A checked command that finishes inside the limit keeps its own exit status and output, and the installer's verification result is unchanged from the documented behaviour.
After a timed-out run and after a successful run, no watchdog process from the check and no private `forgel-code-check` directory remain.
The bounded wait for the watchdog decision terminates on its own, so no run of `install.sh` blocks indefinitely.
`sh -n install.sh` reports no syntax error and the script contains no invocation of GNU `timeout`.
The new regression test fails against the current `bounded_run` and passes against the fixed one.
`python -m pytest -q` passes for the whole repository.

external_dependencies.name: POSIX shell (`/bin/sh`, dash, bash, zsh, ksh)
external_dependencies.interface: Execute `install.sh` as a POSIX shell script: the suite runs the real `install.sh` as a subprocess through `/bin/sh` (or the script's shebang) — argv, stdin/stdout/stderr and exit status only; the installer and tests additionally start login interactive shells as `-l -i -c` invocations of the available shell (`/bin/sh`, dash, bash, zsh, ksh). No emulation layer is needed because the concrete shell executable is provided by the host environment.
external_dependencies.docs: POSIX.1-2017 Shell Command Language; repository contract quoted in the header of `install.sh`
external_dependencies.evidence: The header of `install.sh` states the POSIX shell contract for the script, and `tests/test_install.py` executes the real `install.sh` as a subprocess, so the shell is consumed only through its standard process interface.

result.summary: Made the watchdog's timeout decision authoritative in `bounded_run` and proved it with a real-installer regression test. The watchdog now records its decision in the private check directory (`timed-out` when the bound elapsed before the checked command exited, `finished` when the command won the race), and `bounded_run` waits with a new `await_decision` helper — bounded by `DECISION_WAIT`, derived from `VERIFY_GRACE` — before reading the outcome. A `timed-out` decision forces `CHECK_STATUS=124` regardless of the ordering between the child's exit and the marker write; a missing decision within the wait is also treated as 124, never as success, so a silent watchdog cannot turn a timed-out check into a pass nor hang the installer. The success path keeps the checked command's own exit status and captured output untouched. `verify_profile` reports 124 through `verification_failure`, which names the configured limit. `bounded_run` releases the watchdog, the checked process tree and the private directory on every exit path (including the failure and timeout paths), and the header comment now describes the decision-based bounded check. Added `InstallerBoundedTimeoutDecisionTest` in `tests/test_install.py`, which drives the real `install.sh` with a fresh-shell stand-in that outlives `FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT=1` and prints a success report, asserting a non-zero install, the `stopped after 1s` failure message, no success output and no leftover check directory; a second case covers a watchdog decision that never arrives. Verified with `python -m pytest -q` (204 passed, 137 subtests), `python -m pytest tests/test_install.py -k 'BoundedTimeoutDecision or Watchdog or BoundedCheck or BoundedTools'` (9 passed), and the suite's own `sh -n install.sh` and no-GNU-`timeout` checks.; uncommitted files outside the contract: install.sh, tests/test_install.py

command: outlives or never_arrives or bounded or timeout
BoundedTimeoutDecision or Watchdog or BoundedCheck or BoundedTools

assumptions: The existing `VERIFY_GRACE=2` is a sufficient upper bound for waiting on the watchdog's decision, exposed as `DECISION_WAIT` with a floor of one second; no new configuration variable was introduced.
The watchdog writes its decision before it starts signalling, so waiting for the decision and then `wait`ing on the watchdog keeps the timeout path free of leftover processes.

A test stand-in named like a handled shell (a `bash` stub in a temporary directory used as `$SHELL`) is the way to make the real `install.sh` run a fresh-shell check whose runtime deterministically exceeds a one-second bound.
